notable_absence.finding: The example's whole premise is that a two-keyspace JOIN needs two credential sets, which implies a per-keyspace authorization model - but the page never states which privilege on which keyspace either identity supplies, nor why the JOIN could not be satisfied by one sufficiently-privileged user. It also does not state what happens if one of the supplied credentials is valid and the other is not. So the page motivates multi-credential authentication with an authorization argument it never makes explicit.

cross_component_finding:
TWO DISTINCT AUTHENTICATION MECHANISMS ON ONE API, WITH A PRECEDENCE RULE STATED ON NEITHER PAGE. Taken together, exauthhttp.md and exauthrequest.md establish that the Query Service REST API accepts credentials two ways: in the HTTP Basic Authentication header, or in the request body via the creds parameter. These are not stylistic alternatives - they have different capabilities. The header mechanism can carry exactly one credential; creds is the only mechanism that can carry several. That capability difference is the reason both exist, and it is the modelling contribution: authenticatesVia now has two objects for one subject, disambiguated by mustUseInsteadWhen rather than by version or edition.

What neither example page says, and what a reader following only this directory cannot discover, is which mechanism wins when both are present. The downstream reference page states it unambiguously: server/current/n1ql-rest-query/index.md, Security section - "The Query Service API accepts credentials via HTTP basic authentication header, or via the `creds` request parameter. If a request contains both HTTP basic authentication header and a `creds` parameter, the `creds` parameter is ignored and only the HTTP basic authentication header is used for authenticating." The same page's creds parameter table entry repeats it: "If credentials are supplied in the request header, then HTTP Basic Authentication takes precedence and creds is ignored." That same reference page also confirms the identity-type vocabulary modelled here: "The Query API supports two types of identity: local (or bucket) and admin." I have not filed the precedence rule as a relation on this record because the evidence is not quotable from this page; reconciliation should attach it to the n1ql-rest-query record when that page is extracted, using a predicate of the shape takesPrecedenceOver (absent from the registry - the nearest existing predicates are mustUseInsteadWhen, which expresses obligation rather than override, and incompatibleWithCredentialType, which expresses mutual exclusion rather than a silent winner). "Silently ignored when both are present" is a distinct and common API shape worth its own predicate.

On the identity prefix: the registry has appliesToRoleWhenPrefixed and sgw:role-name-prefix-convention from the Sync Gateway rounds, i.e. it already knows about prefix conventions carrying semantics. The Query creds prefix is the same *technique* applied to a different thing (selecting a user's identity domain, not scoping a role name), so I have kept it as a separate id. The parallel is worth recording because a prefix-convention pattern now appears in two unrelated components, which suggests a reusable modelling shape rather than two one-offs.
version_finding: None on this page. Worth noting for reconciliation, though, that the creds parameter is the kind of feature that usually attracts a deprecation notice - it passes passwords in a request body/query string - and neither this page nor the n1ql-rest-query parameter table marks it deprecated in 8.0. Recording the absence of a deprecation marker deliberately, since this wave exists to build deprecation vocabulary: creds is a live, undeprecated mechanism as of Server 8.0.
